bib.title: Minimax Lower Bounds for Stochastic Linear Bandits (Chapter 24, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: book chapter (Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press), pp. 288-295

question: What is the best worst-case (minimax) regret any policy can guarantee for stochastic linear bandits, depending on the action set, sparsity and misspecification?
contributions: Hypercube lower bound Omega(d sqrt n) showing Chapter 19 upper bounds cannot be improved in general
Unit-ball lower bound of the same order
Sparse lower bound Omega(sqrt(p d n)) matching Chapter 23 up to logs
Impossibility of adaptive bounds for misspecified linear bandits

results.claim: On the hypercube action set, every policy suffers regret of order d*sqrt(n) on some parameter in Theta, so the Chapter 19 upper bound is near optimal up to logs.
results.setup: A=[-1,1]^d, Theta={-n^-1/2, n^-1/2}^d, unit-variance Gaussian noise, any policy; regret >= (exp(-2)/8) d sqrt(n) for some theta. exp(-2)/8 is about 0.017, so the constant is small.
results.quote: Except for logarithmic factors, this shows that the algorithm of Chapter 19

results.claim: Unit-ball lower bound: some theta with squared norm d^2/(48n) forces regret d sqrt(n)/(16 sqrt 3).
results.setup: A = unit ball in R^d, d <= 2n, Gaussian noise, any policy; the same proof works for the unit sphere.
results.quote: The same proof works when A = {x ∈Rd : ∥x∥2 = 1} is the unit sphere.
results.note: Theorem prints 48n for the norm and 16 sqrt3 in the bound

results.claim: Sparse linear bandit with sparsity p in ambient dimension d: regret lower bound sqrt(p d n)/8, so sparsity cannot remove polynomial dependence on d.
results.setup: A = p copies of k-armed bandits (d=pk, multi-task: only the summed reward is seen), pd <= n, ||theta||_0 = p; matches Chapter 23 upper bound O~(sqrt(d) sqrt(p n)) up to logs.
results.quote:
Except for logarithmic
terms this bound cannot be improved.

results.claim: With p=1 the sparse problem reduces to the finite-armed bandit with minimax regret of order sqrt(dn).
results.setup: p=1 case of sparse bandit; see Chapter 15.
results.quote: essentially reduces to the ﬁnite-armed bandit problem where the minimax regret

results.claim: Adaptive bounds for misspecified models are impossible: a policy with regret O(sqrt n) when the model is exactly linear (d=1 embedding) must suffer Omega(k sqrt n) on some general k-armed instance.
results.setup: Finite-armed bandit, means in [0,1]^k, 2(k-1) <= V <= sqrt(n(k-1) exp(-2))/8, sup over Theta of regret <= V; implies the desired bound min{d sqrt n + eps n, sqrt(kn)} is not achievable.
results.quote: It follows that Eq. (24.7) is a pipe dream.

results.claim: Achievable misspecified rates: O~(d sqrt n + eps n sqrt d) for large k (essentially unimprovable), and O~(sqrt(dkn) + eps n sqrt k) for small k (Foster and Rakhlin 2020).
results.setup: misspecification error eps = sup_a |<theta,a> - mu(a)|, finite action set size k.

limits: All bounds are worst-case over a chosen hard action set and parameter set, with Gaussian unit-variance noise; they say nothing about instance-dependent regret.
Optimal regret for a wide range of action sets is an open question (Notes 1).
The optimal tradeoff for misspecified bandits is open; the authors only speculate a policy with regret O~(min{(d sqrt n + eps n sqrt d), (k/d) sqrt n}) for k >= d^2.
Constants are small (e.g. exp(-2)/8) and not tight; lower bound hides logs.
practices: Read a minimax bound as a statement about the worst parameter for an action set: for hypercube, ball and sphere, expect regret of order d*sqrt(n) (Sec 24.1-24.2).
Do not expect sparsity to beat polynomial dependence on d: regret scales with sqrt(p d n) (Sec 24.3).
When the linear model may be misspecified, accept O~(d sqrt n + eps n sqrt d) rather than hoping for an adaptive min with sqrt(kn) (Sec 24.4, Notes 2).

terms.definition: the learner plays p finite-armed bandits simultaneously but observes only the sum of the rewards, with noise added at the end
the mean rewards are not assumed to follow a linear model exactly; epsilon is sup_a |<theta,a> - mu(a)| for the best theta
proof device: average the per-coordinate failure probability over all theta in Theta so some theta is bad for many coordinates at once
